abstract_en: Drug-induced QT/QTc prolongation is a central component of cardiac safety assessment. Concentration-QT/QTc modelling uses measured or model-predicted systemic drug exposure to estimate the magnitude and uncertainty of effects on ventricular repolarisation and can support regulatory decision-making in early clinical development. However, the evidence is dispersed across dedicated thorough QT studies, early-phase studies, population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic analyses, and secondary pooled analyses, with substantial variation in exposure metrics, electrocardiographic acquisition, heart-rate correction, model structure, assessment of active metabolites and delayed effects, and reporting of uncertainty. This protocol describes a systematic review of quantitative human concentration-QT/QTc evidence. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Google Scholar will be searched from inception without date or language restrictions. Original human studies will be eligible when drug or metabolite concentrations are measured or estimated from a pharmacokinetic model informed by study data and are quantitatively related to QT or QTc outcomes. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and assess methodological limitations. The primary estimands will be the concentration-QT/QTc drug-effect parameter and the predicted placebo-adjusted change from baseline in QTc at a clinically relevant exposure. Random-effects meta-analysis will be undertaken only within the same active moiety when analyte, endpoint, correction method, model estimand, and exposure scenario are sufficiently comparable; otherwise, structured synthesis without meta-analysis will be performed. Risk of bias will be assessed using design-appropriate tools where applicable, supplemented by a prespecified concentration-QT/QTc methodological framework. Certainty will be evaluated for coherent drug-specific bodies of evidence. This review will provide a transparent map of clinical concentration-QT/QTc methods and estimates and identify priorities for future cardiac safety studies. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261469142.
abstract_es: Abstract

La prolongación del QT/QTc inducida por fármacos es un componente central de la evaluación de la seguridad cardíaca. La modelización de la concentración-QT/QTc utiliza la exposición sistémica medida o predicha por modelos para estimar la magnitud e incertidumbre de los efectos sobre la repolarización ventricular y puede apoyar la toma de decisiones reguladoras en el desarrollo clínico temprano. Sin embargo, la evidencia se dispersa en estudios específicos exhaustivos de QT, estudios de fase temprana, análisis farmacodinámicos poblacionales y análisis secundarios agrupados, con una variación sustancial en las métricas de exposición, adquisición electrocardiográfica, corrección de la frecuencia cardíaca, estructura de modelos, evaluación de metabolitos activos y efectos retardados, y notificación de incertidumbre. Este protocolo describe una revisión sistemática de la concentración cuantitativa humana-QT/QTc evidencia. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, el Registro Central Cochrane de Ensayos Controlados, ClinicalTrials.gov y Google Scholar se buscarán desde el principio sin restricciones de fecha ni idioma. Los estudios en humanos originales serán elegibles cuando se midan o se calculen las concentraciones de fármaco o metabolitos a partir de un modelo farmacocinético basado en los datos del estudio y estén cuantitativamente relacionados con los resultados del QT o QTc. Dos revisores analizarán de forma independiente los registros, extraerán datos y evaluarán las limitaciones metodológicas. Los estimandos primarios serán el parámetro de efecto farmacológico de la concentración-QT/QTc y el cambio previsto ajustado por placebo respecto al valor basal en QTc a una exposición clínicamente relevante. El metaanálisis de efectos aleatorios sólo se realizará dentro de la misma fracción activa cuando el analito, el criterio de valoración, el método de corrección, la estimación del modelo y el escenario de exposición sean suficientemente comparables; de lo contrario, se realizará una síntesis estructurada sin metaanálisis. El riesgo de sesgo se evaluará utilizando herramientas apropiadas para el diseño, cuando proceda, complementadas con un marco metodológico de concentración preespecificada-QT/QTc. Se evaluará la certeza para cuerpos de evidencia coherentes específicos del fármaco. Esta revisión proporcionará un mapa transparente de los métodos de concentración clínica-QT/QTc y estimaciones e identificará las prioridades para futuros estudios de seguridad cardíaca.

abstract_en:
Background
Arrhythmias are often associated with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity, which significantly influence their onset and progression. In this context, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have garnered attention for their potential benefits, with emerging evidence indicating that GLP-1 receptor activation might offer antiarrhythmic effects.Objectives
This study aimed to evaluate the impact of all GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists on the incidence of new-onset arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF).Methods
A comprehensive search of databases was conducted from inception to December 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on patients with diabetes or obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs or co-agonists. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Interventions were ranked using the p-score cumulative rank, ranging from 0 (worst) to 1 (best).Results
A total of 94 RCTs involving 155,989 patients were included, comparing 12 GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists. Subcutaneous semaglutide emerged as the most effective intervention, significantly reducing AF incidence compared with placebo (RR 0.82; 95% CI: 0.68 to 0.99), and compared with tirzepatide (RR 0.57; 95% CI: 0.37 to 0.88). In contrast, dulaglutide was associated with an increased risk of AF, while lixisenatide was associated with a decreased risk in atrioventricular blocks. For AF, semaglutide presented a p-score of 0.7885, while tirzepatide and dulaglutide scored 0.1830 and 0.1750, respectively.Conclusion
Among GLP-1 RAs and co-agonists, subcutaneous semaglutide is highlighted as the most effective intervention for reducing the risk of AF. Further studies focusing on arrhythmic outcomes are needed to confirm these findings.

Aim
Lifestyle modification is crucial for cardiovascular disease prevention but remains challenging due to complex behavioural factors such as the intention-behaviour gap. Digital commitment devices (DCD) could narrow this gap by leveraging behavioural economics, but its effectiveness remains unclear. Therefore, this review aims to evaluate the effects of DCDs on lifestyle and cardiometabolic outcomes in adults with elevated cardiometabolic risk.Methods
A systematic search of 12 electronic databases was conducted from database inception to August 2025. Study selection and methodological quality appraisal using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool were performed independently by two reviewers. Where appropriate, effect sizes were pooled using random effects meta-analyses. The certainty of evidence for meta-analysed outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach.Results

DCDs could improve lifestyle and cardiometabolic outcomes by improving physical activity and weight management, thus enhancing cardiometabolic disease prevention. Future research should prioritise long-term trials with extended follow-up periods beyond 12 months to observe physiological improvements and assess maintenance of effects.

abstract_en:
Background
Respiratory muscle training interventions have shown promising results in improving functional capacity, quality of life, and prognosis of heart failure patients. However, the optimal respiratory muscle training intervention for rehabilitation remains unclear.Methods
A systematic review and network meta-analysis was conducted by searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library until September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effect of respiratory muscle training interventions on maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP), maximum expiratory pressure (MEP), forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁), six-minute walk test (6MWT), peak oxygen uptake (VO2max), quality of life, and dyspnea. Random-effect network meta-analysis was used to estimate pooled mean differences. Interventions were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).Results
A total of 88 RCTs (5,757 participants) were included. Medium-intensity inspiratory muscle training (IMT) ranked highest for improving MIP (SUCRA: 89.8%). Combined aerobic and resistance exercise was optimal for MEP (SUCRA: 79.3%). Aerobic training showed the greatest benefit for FVC (SUCRA: 94.8%) and FEV₁ (SUCRA: 93.8%). Medium-intensity IMT was most effective for enhancing 6MWT performance (SUCRA: 81.6%). A combination of high-intensity IMT with aerobic training yielded the largest gains in improving VO2max (SUCRA: 74.7%), quality of life (SUCRA: 81.4%), and reducing dyspnea (SUCRA: 89.3%).Conclusion
Respiratory muscle training interventions provide different benefits across key rehabilitation outcomes in heart failure. Accordingly, rehabilitation strategies may be optimized by aligning exercise modalities with patients' rehabilitation needs, preferences, and clinical profiles, rather than adopting a uniform prescription.
